Chapter 2: Life Under the Regime—Daily Struggles and the Weight of Control
Imagine stepping into a world where every promise quickly unravels. That’s what happened when the family tried to settle in North Korea. The government’s presence was everywhere—controlling food, jobs, and even the way people thought. Each morning started with the same old routines: forced meetings, public shows of loyalty, and that overwhelming sense that someone was always watching.
Can you picture living in a place where your neighbors might report you, and even kids learned not to trust their friends? That was their everyday reality.
Food was never enough. From the very start, hunger was just part of life. The mother, who used to make meals stretch back in Japan, now faced empty shelves and endless lines. The father—hoping for a fresh start—lost his sense of purpose and dignity, picking up any work he could find, but it still wasn’t enough. The kids got used to feeling hungry, and learned to hide their disappointment so it wouldn’t worry their parents.
School didn’t offer any escape. Lessons were all about praising the leader and warning kids about enemies. The boy, who already stood out, just couldn’t keep up. Teachers demanded total obedience, and even a hint of doubt could get you in trouble. Making friends was risky, because trust could be traded for a handful of extra rations or a bit of praise from an official. So, the boy learned to keep his thoughts—and his fears—to himself.
Being returnees made everything harder. They were always outsiders, always suspected of not being loyal enough. The father’s Korean heritage offered no real protection, and the mother’s Japanese background made things even worse. The family got the worst jobs and the poorest housing. People expected them to be grateful, but honestly, gratitude was a tough ask when every day felt like a battle.
As the years went by, the regime’s grip only got tighter. Propaganda was everywhere—on the radio, plastered across walls, and echoing in the streets. Every home had to display portraits of the leader, and showing anything less than perfect respect could get you punished. The family went through the motions, performing the rituals of loyalty, but inside, disappointment and anger grew. The father’s frustration simmered, while the mother’s sadness deepened.
Still, every now and then, a little bit of kindness would shine through. Maybe a neighbor shared a handful of rice, or a teacher quietly looked the other way when a child slipped up. These moments were rare, but they meant the world. They reminded the family that, even in the harshest conditions, people could still find ways to care for each other.
But survival came at a steep price. The family had to hide what they really felt, say what was expected, and accept the things they couldn’t change. The boy, once so hopeful, grew cautious and wary. He saw friends disappear—sometimes for small mistakes, sometimes for no reason at all. The fear of being singled out was always there, lurking in the background.
The real power of the regime wasn’t just in its strict rules. It was in the way it shaped how people thought and felt. Over time, the family’s dreams got smaller and smaller. Survival became the only thing that mattered. Still, deep down, the boy—now growing into a young man—couldn’t quite let go of hope. He knew it was dangerous, but the desire for freedom and dignity just wouldn’t fade, no matter how dark the world around him became.
